actual_output:
In the context of humanoid dodgeball, advanced sensory feedback and Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) work together to enhance evasive maneuvers significantly. The PAC-MAN framework integrates these elements to address the challenges posed by a fast-moving object, such as a dodgeball, which requires rapid and coordinated responses from the robot.

The sensory feedback is primarily derived from a head-mounted depth camera that provides a segmentation-masked view of the incoming ball. This limited perception necessitates that the robot must infer the threat and react quickly to avoid contact while maintaining balance. The paper emphasizes that "the robot must perceive an incoming ball, determine which links are threatened, and coordinate the torso, arms, and legs quickly enough to avoid contact while remaining upright" [4]. This highlights the critical role of sensory input in informing the robot's evasive actions.

CBFs contribute to this process by encoding safety constraints that ensure the robot avoids collisions. They allow the policy to internalize safety structures based on the available sensory information. The study distinguishes between two types of CBFs: Link-CBF, which provides lightweight per-link guidance during training, and Joint-CBF, which offers a more comprehensive whole-body safety framework. The findings indicate that "stronger barrier structure needs more informative observations," suggesting that the effectiveness of CBFs is contingent upon the quality of sensory feedback [4].

Moreover, the integration of an adversarial motion prior (AMP) serves to regularize the robot's evasive movements, favoring naturalistic motions like crouching and sidestepping over arbitrary joint movements. This combination of sensory feedback and CBFs allows the robot to execute evasive maneuvers that are not only reactive but also grounded in learned human-like motion patterns, enhancing the overall effectiveness of the evasive strategy in dodgeball scenarios [5].

In summary, the collaboration between advanced sensory feedback and CBFs in the PAC-MAN framework enables humanoid robots to perform complex evasive maneuvers effectively, ensuring both safety and balance in dynamic environments.

Motion imitation and priors for humanoid control. Motion imitation has long provided a practical route to naturalistic, high-dimensional control. [12] showed that RL can track reference motions reliably, [13] replaced explicit tracking with an adversarial discriminator over motion features, which yields a style reward compatible with a task objective, and [14], [15] learned reusable skill and style embeddings over large motion datasets. Recent wholebody tracking systems move closer to our humanoid setting:

Retargeting quality also matters here, both for general humanoid tracking [21] and for interaction-preserving loco-manipulation [22]. For dodgeball, a motion prior is attractive because the reward for 'not being hit' is too semantically sparse and geometric to specify how a humanoid should move. We select human dodging motions as priors and also condition the policy on a perception stream, thus combining the motion prior with exteroceptive information to produce whole-body evasive reflexes.

Section: Perception-aware safety, parkour, and fast-object tasks.

The closest conceptual neighbor to perception-aware dodgeball is safe agility under partial exteroception. Quadruped parkour [23], [24] and agile-but-safe locomotion [8] show how perception, skill selection, recovery, and safety layers can support fast motion around obstacles, while humanoid parkour and perception-aware locomotion systems [2], [25][27] extend this to higher-dimensional bodies with depthor elevation-conditioned policies for jumping, leaping, and terrain traversal. Related work studies the same perception-speed-stability tradeoff through depth conditioning [7], online policy switching [28], and active gaze [29]. Dodgeball differs from these terrain-centered settings because the hazard is a fast-moving object rather than traversable terrain. The ball may be visible only briefly, so the policy must forecast imminent body contact and produce an evasive whole-body response instead of merely choosing footholds. Task-centered fast-object work makes this timing pressure explicit: [30] uses humanoid table tennis to study sub-second ball prediction, task planning, and whole-body RL control. Whole-body avoidance and safety. Reactive safety spans both recovering balance after a disturbance via capture-point and push-recovery control [31], [32], and avoiding contact in the first place via control barrier functions [10], collisionfree MPC [33], and fast collision-free motion generation [34]. Most related to our safety treatment, [11] injects safety structure during humanoid training and removes the runtime filter at deployment, and [9] concurrently explores egocentric tactile and proximity sensing as a modality complementary to the vision used here. We study depth-based dodgeball on the Unitree G1, using perception-aware CBF-RL to couple onboard visual observations with per-link safety guidance and motion-regularized whole-body evasion.

Section: I. INTRODUCTION

Humanoid robots operating around moving objects must react within a fraction of a second, and the evasion itself must not cost them their balance. Dodgeball isolates this safety problem in a short-horizon, whole-body setting: the robot must perceive an incoming ball, determine which links are threatened, and coordinate the torso, arms, and legs quickly enough to avoid contact while remaining upright. Humans solve the same problem by keeping their eyes on the ball and moving their whole body out of its path. Recent learning-based controllers can produce dynamic humanoid locomotion [1], [2], whole-body imitation [3]-[5], and visually conditioned skills [6], [7], but reactive whole-body safety from onboard vision remains difficult [8], [9], especially for a humanoid.
Control barrier functions (CBFs) encode collision-free sets and correct unsafe commands, provided the relevant state is available [10]. Onboard perception breaks this convenient assumption: the incoming object may be visible only briefly, may leave the camera field of view, or may appear as a few noisy depth pixels. CBF-RL can move barrier information into policy training [11], but a deployed policy can internalize only as much safety structure as its observations support. actual_output:
Cost-aware abstention in IT ticket routing methodologies is influenced by several critical factors, primarily centered around the costs associated with different routing decisions and the performance of the classifiers used.

1. **Cost Structure**: The methodology hinges on an asymmetric cost structure where the costs for routing decisions are distinctly defined. The costs include:
   - **c_ok**: Cost of a correct auto-route, which is effectively zero.
   - **c_triage**: Cost of human triage, set at one.
   - **c_wrong**: Cost of an incorrect auto-route, significantly higher at five. This cost structure emphasizes that misrouting is much more expensive than human intervention, motivating the need for careful decision-making in routing tickets [1][4].

2. **Classifier Performance**: The effectiveness of the routing policy is contingent on the performance of the classifiers. The study compares various classifiers, including traditional models and large language models (LLMs), under different prompting conditions. The results indicate that while LLMs can be effective, their calibration and confidence levels often do not align with actual accuracy, necessitating a careful evaluation of when to trust automated decisions [5].

3. **Calibration and Sensitivity Analysis**: The paper emphasizes the importance of calibrating the classifiers to align with the cost structure. A post-hoc sensitivity analysis is performed to explore how different cost parameters affect routing decisions. This analysis helps organizations understand their specific cost dynamics and adjust their routing thresholds accordingly [1][2].

4. **Empirical Framework**: The study provides a reproducible empirical framework that allows organizations to assess whether automatic ticket routing is cost-preferred under their specific assumptions. This framework separates prediction, confidence, rejection, and cost, making it easier to audit each component and adapt to future datasets or cost estimates [2][4].

In summary, the interplay between cost structures, classifier performance, and calibration practices forms the backbone of effective cost-aware abstention in IT ticket routing methodologies, as detailed in the study [1][4].

The critical factors influencing cost-aware abstention in IT ticket routing methodologies include:

1. **Cost Structure**: The asymmetric costs associated with routing decisions—correct routes incur no cost, human triage costs one unit, and incorrect routes cost five units—are fundamental in determining when to abstain from auto-routing.

2. **Classifier Calibration**: The calibration of classifiers, particularly large language models (LLMs), is crucial. Poorly calibrated models may produce high confidence values that do not reflect actual accuracy, leading to costly misroutes.

3. **Threshold Selection**: The selection of thresholds based on calibration data is essential for minimizing expected costs. For instance, a threshold of 0.60 was found to significantly reduce costs and wrong routes in the study.

These factors collectively inform the decision-making process regarding when to trust automated routing versus deferring to human triage.

Section: Cost-Aware Abstention for LLM-Based IT Ticket Classification

Sachin Gupta Independent Researcher United States sachinkg12@gmail.com
Abstract -Wrong automatic routing of an IT support ticket can cost more than human triage. We evaluate cost-aware abstention as an offline, cost-conditional readiness assessment: a routing policy is selected on calibration data under asymmetric costs and evaluated once on held-out test data. On a public 47,837ticket, eight-class corpus, we compare four trained classifiers with four large language models under zero- and few-shot prompting. With illustrative per-ticket costs of zero for a correct route, one for human triage, and five for a wrong route, term-frequencyinverse-document-frequency logistic regression selects a threshold of 0.60 and reduces test cost from 0.763 to 0.472, a 38.1 % relative reduction (95 % bootstrap confidence interval, 35.7 %40.4 %), while lowering wrong routes from 15.3 % to 3.5 %. In a post-hoc 16-setting analysis, calibration-selected policies beat both always-route and always-defer in 14 settings. The strongest prompted configuration reaches 0.477 accuracy on a stratified 1,000-ticket subset, versus 0.879 for fine-tuned DistilBERT on the same tickets. Isotonic recalibration reduces expected calibration error but does not reliably improve ranking discrimination; one GPT-4o-mini setting emits a single confidence value and has correctness area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.500. At the break-even probability of 0.80, seven prompted conditions defer every ticket, and Haiku few-shot routes 19 of 1,000. A language-model-only agreement control and margin- and entropy-based rejection scores for the logistic-regression baseline provide nontrivial comparators. The findings are scoped to this dataset, prompt design, model endpoints, and illustrative costs; the work is an evaluation framework, not a new abstention algorithm or universal deployment certification.
Index Terms -trustworthy machine learning, calibration, costaware abstention, selective prediction, large language models, text classification, IT service management

Cost-Aware Abstention for LLM-Based IT Ticket Classification

Section: I. INTRODUCTION

Enterprise IT service desks process tens of thousands of internal tickets per month, where the 'customer' is an employee asking internal IT for help with hardware, access, or software (not an external consumer). HDI/MetricNet reports the North American average cost per voice IT service-desk ticket at US$17.19, with walk-up tickets averaging US$37.52 [1]. Routing happens under an asymmetric cost structure. Sending a ticket to the correct queue is nearly free. Sending it to a human triager is moderately costly. Sending it to the wrong queue is much more expensive once you account for handoff latency, double work, and missed service levels. Accuracy or macro-F1 alone cannot represent this asymmetry or indicate when to trust an automated decision [2], [3].
Two trends make this gap more pressing. First, large language models (LLMs) can be prompted as zero- or few-shot text classifiers [4], [5], potentially reducing the need for taskspecific training. Second, modern neural classifiers, including LLMs, are known to be poorly calibrated. They often produce high confidence values regardless of actual accuracy [6]-[9]. Together these trends raise a concrete operational question: should a prompted LLM be allowed to auto-route IT tickets, and if so, under what abstention policy?
We study this question on the public IT Service Ticket Classification Dataset (47,837 tickets, eight categories). We treat cost-aware abstention not as a way to improve a classifier but as an empirical readiness test under stated assumptions. Predictors, confidence estimators, rejection scores, and policies remain separate. Our contributions are:
A comparison of four trained non-LLM classifiers and eight prompted LLM conditions on the same public corpus, including a common 1,000-ticket test subset.
A calibration analysis that reports expected calibration error (ECE), correctness area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), and tie-aware area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC), plus separate mixed ( M =9 ) and LLM-only ( M =8 ) agreement pools.
A calibration-selected, paired-bootstrap cost analysis with top-probability, probability-margin, and entropy rejection scores; a post-hoc 16-setting cost-parameter analysis; and LLM policies that use a cost-derived threshold rather than test tuning.
A reproducible evaluation framework and per-ticket artifacts that expose prediction, confidence, rejection, and cost as separately auditable stages.
The main observation is simple: abstention does not repair a weak classifier. It exposes when auto-routing is cost-preferred under a particular dataset, confidence signal, and cost model.
Positioning. The components we combine are individually established: Chow-style error-reject [3], Elkan-style costsensitive decision-making [10], ECE-based calibration diagnostics [6], [11], isotonic recalibration, and self-consistencyinspired agreement signals [12]. We introduce no new abstention algorithm. This paper's contribution is an empirical evaluation of deployment-relevant assumptions and its reproducible implementation, not a universal readiness certificate.

II. RELATED WORK

Selective prediction and abstention. The classical framework for rejecting uncertain inputs traces back to Chow's error-reject trade-off [3]. It has been formalized for modern classifiers under the names selective prediction [2], [13] and learning with abstention [14]; a recent survey organizes LLM abstention methods, benchmarks, and evaluation metrics [15]. The closest line is learning to defer , where a classifier is trained jointly with the option to pass an instance to a human expert [16], [17]. Our training-free confidence-threshold policy addresses the same route-or-defer action space without joint training. We evaluate its decisions under an explicit cost model following Elkan's cost-sensitive formulation [10].

Calibration and overconfidence. Guo et al. [6] documented systematic overconfidence in deep neural classifiers and popularized Expected Calibration Error (ECE) [11] as a diagnostic. A growing literature studies whether LLMs are well-calibrated [7]-[9], [18]. The broad finding is that verbalized confidence runs too high. We contribute a publicdataset measurement of LLM ECE in an asymmetric-cost classification setting, and report agreement-across-predictors as a confidence signal inspired by self-consistency [12].

LLMs for text classification. Off-the-shelf prompting of LLMs as classifiers [4], [5], [19] is operationally attractive, but on short, lexical-signal-heavy tasks strong classical text classifiers such as linear SVMs [20] remain highly competitive, as our IT-ticket results confirm (§V-A). Cost-driven LLM cascades and routing lower inference cost by escalating only hard inputs to a stronger model [21]; we instead hold the model fixed and use abstention to decide when not to auto-route at all. Our evaluation lands in the same mixed picture for the IT-ticket domain.

IT ticket classification. Automated routing of support tickets has a long applications-track history [22], [23] but is rarely evaluated under explicit cost models or with abstention. Our framework is structured as a deferral layer that could be integrated into an IT service management pipeline rather than as a new classifier.

The assessment of cost-sensitive abstention strategies in IT ticket routing, particularly under asymmetric cost dynamics, is thoroughly explored in the paper "Cost-Aware Abstention for LLM-Based IT Ticket Classification" (arXiv:2610.31657v1). The authors emphasize that incorrect automatic routing of IT support tickets can incur higher costs than human triage, leading to the evaluation of cost-aware abstention as a viable strategy.

The study employs a framework that categorizes decisions into three cost types: correct auto-routing (c_ok), human triage (c_triage), and incorrect auto-routing (c_wrong), with illustrative costs set at (0, 1, 5). This setup reflects the qualitative understanding that misrouting is significantly more costly than human intervention. The authors demonstrate that a calibration-selected TF-IDF + logistic regression policy can reduce the modeled cost by 38.1%, showcasing its effectiveness in a public dataset of 47,837 tickets across eight classes. The policy also notably decreased the rate of incorrect routes from 15.3% to 3.5% [1][2].

In a post-hoc analysis, the authors found that their calibration-selected policies outperformed both always-routing and always-defer strategies in 14 out of 16 settings. This indicates that a well-calibrated approach to abstention can lead to substantial cost savings and improved decision-making in ticket routing scenarios. However, they caution that the findings are specific to the dataset, prompt design, and model endpoints used, and they stress the importance of organizations estimating their own cost dynamics before applying these strategies [1][4].

Overall, the paper provides a structured evaluation framework for cost-sensitive abstention, highlighting its potential benefits while acknowledging the need for tailored cost assessments in different organizational contexts.

input: How does the per-prompt n-gram cache improve drafting efficiency while adapting to policy changes and maintaining memory constraints during training?
actual_output:
The per-prompt n-gram cache in NgramRL significantly enhances drafting efficiency by leveraging the temporal locality of rollouts from reinforcement learning (RL) post-training. Each prompt maintains its own n-gram look-up table (LUT), which is constructed from prior rollouts. This design allows the cache to propose continuations based on previously observed sequences, effectively utilizing the redundancy in rollouts that occur across training epochs. As noted in the paper, "across consecutive epochs, a prior rollout covers 48-96% of a later rollout," indicating that the cache can provide high-quality drafts that align closely with the evolving policy's preferences [3].

The cache is continually updated with recent rollouts, ensuring it remains aligned with the current policy without requiring retraining. This self-updating behavior allows the drafter to adapt to policy changes dynamically, as it "tracks the policy without retraining" by retaining only the most relevant entries from a bounded history window [1]. The design choice to implement per-prompt caching rather than a single global cache is crucial; it enhances acceptance rates significantly, achieving up to 3.05 accepted tokens per step compared to only 2.41 with a global cache [4].

Moreover, the memory constraints are managed effectively through the bounded history window, which limits the number of rollouts retained. This approach not only saves memory but also ensures that the cache remains relevant, as older rollouts may become stale and less useful for current policy verification [4]. Overall, the per-prompt n-gram cache optimizes both drafting speed and memory efficiency, making it a powerful tool in the NgramRL framework for structured generation tasks [2].

Section: 1 Introduction

Reinforcement learning post-training [17, 19], and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) in particular [20], has become central to improving LLM reasoning [6]. But it is expensive, and the cost is dominated by the rollout generation. Each GRPO step autoregressively samples many completions per prompt before any gradient is To this end, we propose NgramRL, a rollout-aware per-prompt n-gram cache that acts as a model-free drafter for speculative decoding during RL post-training. For each prompt, NgramRL maintains an n-gram table built from that prompt's prior rollouts and proposes continuations by lookup, which the policy verifies. The cache lives in host memory and is queried on the CPU, overlapping GPU computation so that drafting adds no persistent GPU memory and negligible GPU time, and because it is populated by the policy's own outputs it stays aligned with the policy rather than going stale like a fixed drafter. To keep this CPU work off the critical path, NgramRL pairs the cache with an asynchronous multipath prefetch runtime that prefetches the next step's drafts during verification, so the decode iteration collapses to GPU busy time.

We design an adaptive fan-out prefetcher, guided by a causal budget allocator, that speculatively prepares nextstep drafts for likely verification outcomes ( 𝑗, 𝑏 ) during the forward. Covered outcomes bypass the verificationdependent host round trip; uncovered requests fall back to sequential lookup without altering the target-emitted token or rollout distribution.
Across two model families and three workloads, NgramRL commits 3.60-7.77 tokens per target-model forward in the warm-cache regime, up to 1 . 99 × more than SuffixDecoding and 7 . 0 × more than prompt-lookup decoding. At 𝑁 = 16, the prefetcher covers up to 99.5% of Spider outcomes and delivers up to 1 . 38 × measured rollout speedup over synchronous NgramRL.

The design rests on one property of RL post-training. GRPO [20] revisits the same prompts across steps and epochs, and the policy changes only incrementally between them, so a prompt's completions repeat those it produced earlier in training. Figure 2 illustrates this phenomenon: rollouts of the same Spider [23] (text-to-SQL) prompt one epoch apart share only the query skeleton early on and become verbatim identical by late training. NgramRL turns this redundancy into accepted drafts, a signal a single-generation drafter cannot utilize.
Each prompt owns an 𝑛 -gram cache built from its prior rollouts. During rollout the cache proposes continuations by lookup and the policy verifies them exactly, preserving the output distribution. The cache lives in host memory and is queried on the CPU, so drafting adds no persistent GPU memory and overlaps GPU compute. The remaining subsections detail the cache, the draft-and-verify procedure, and the CPU-GPU co-design.

input: How do acceptance rates differ between per-prompt and global caching methods during NgramRL training?
actual_output:
During NgramRL training, acceptance rates significantly differ between per-prompt and global caching methods. The study demonstrates that using a per-prompt n-gram cache (Cₚ) yields higher acceptance rates compared to a global cache. Specifically, the per-prompt keying approach achieves an acceptance rate of 3.05 tokens per step, while the global cache method results in an acceptance rate of only 2.41 tokens per step, which is comparable to SuffixDecoding at 2.43 tokens per step. This indicates that the per-prompt cache is more effective in capturing relevant continuations from prior rollouts, leading to better performance in speculative decoding tasks [1].

The advantage of per-prompt caching arises from its ability to leverage the repetitive nature of rollouts for the same prompt, which is not as effectively captured by a global cache. The study notes that "rollouts of the same prompt are more repetitive with each other than rollouts of different prompts," making per-prompt caches particularly beneficial for maintaining high acceptance rates [4]. 

Furthermore, the results show that the per-prompt cache's design allows it to adaptively update based on recent rollouts, ensuring that it remains aligned with the evolving policy, while a global cache lacks this specificity and thus does not perform as well [5]. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of cache structure in optimizing acceptance rates during NgramRL training.

Section: 1 Introduction

Reinforcement learning post-training [17, 19], and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) in particular [20], has become central to improving LLM reasoning [6]. But it is expensive, and the cost is dominated by the rollout generation. Each GRPO step autoregressively samples many completions per prompt before any gradient is To this end, we propose NgramRL, a rollout-aware per-prompt n-gram cache that acts as a model-free drafter for speculative decoding during RL post-training. For each prompt, NgramRL maintains an n-gram table built from that prompt's prior rollouts and proposes continuations by lookup, which the policy verifies. The cache lives in host memory and is queried on the CPU, overlapping GPU computation so that drafting adds no persistent GPU memory and negligible GPU time, and because it is populated by the policy's own outputs it stays aligned with the policy rather than going stale like a fixed drafter. To keep this CPU work off the critical path, NgramRL pairs the cache with an asynchronous multipath prefetch runtime that prefetches the next step's drafts during verification, so the decode iteration collapses to GPU busy time.

input: Examine HCPD's role in optimizing item preference alignment for enhanced SID generation via distillation.
actual_output:
Hierarchical Collaborative Preference Distillation (HCPD) plays a crucial role in optimizing item preference alignment, which is essential for enhancing Semantic ID (SID) generation in recommendation systems. HCPD leverages a frozen teacher model, specifically DuoRec, to provide collaborative preferences over candidate items based on user interaction history. This approach allows the model to capture user-specific preference differences effectively, thereby improving the relevance of recommendations.

The process begins with the organization of item SIDs into a prefix tree, where each leaf represents a unique item. HCPD utilizes this structure to define a distillation objective that aligns the teacher's conditional preferences with those of the generator. The conditional KL divergence is computed over legal next tokens, which helps in transferring the teacher's relative preferences among complete items to the alternative branches available at each prefix. This method ensures that the generator's probabilities are normalized over the same legal next-token set, allowing for a more accurate representation of item preferences during the recommendation process [1].

The effectiveness of HCPD is highlighted in the ablation studies, where its removal resulted in significant performance drops across various datasets, indicating its importance in supplementing the standard cross-entropy (CE) supervision with collaborative preferences. Specifically, the absence of HCPD led to a 10.9% decrease in Recall@5, underscoring its role in guiding SID generation through item-level collaborative relations [4].

Moreover, HCPD's design focuses on relative preferences among competing items, which enhances the model's ability to prioritize relevant items at the top of recommendation lists. This is evidenced by the performance improvements observed when using HCPD compared to its variants, demonstrating its effectiveness in optimizing item preference alignment for better recommendation outcomes [3]. 

In summary, HCPD significantly enhances SID generation by aligning item preferences through a structured distillation process, ultimately leading to more effective and personalized recommendations.

HCPD (Hierarchical Collaborative Preference Distillation) plays a crucial role in optimizing item preference alignment for enhanced SID (Semantic Identifier) generation. By leveraging a frozen discriminative recommender as a teacher, HCPD aligns the teacher's and generator's conditional distributions over legal next tokens along ground-truth SID paths. This alignment facilitates the transfer of relative preferences among items, ensuring that the generator effectively captures user-specific preferences based on interaction history.

The theoretical framework established by HCPD decomposes item-level KL divergence into weighted prefix-conditional KL terms, allowing for a more nuanced understanding of item preferences. This approach not only enhances the generator's ability to model inter-item relations but also directly guides SID generation through collaborative preference relations. Experimental results demonstrate that HCPD consistently improves recommendation performance, particularly in prioritizing relevant items, thereby validating its effectiveness in the distillation process.

2 Related Work

2.1 Generative Recommendation

GR uses item tokenization to encode prior knowledge of inter-item relations into SIDs. TIGER [31] pioneered the use of residual quanti- zation in GR to learn semantic codes by reconstructing item content representations. Subsequent research has focused on incorporating collaborative signals into SID and aligning tokenization with recommendation objectives. LETTER [34] introduces collaborative alignment and code diversity regularization, while ETEGRec [22] alternates between tokenizer and recommender updates using alignment objectives. Other studies reconsider how item tokens are organized and represented. ActionPiece [11] learns merge rules over unordered feature sets using co-occurrences within items and across adjacent interactions. SST [26] compresses history-side item tokens into semantic subwords while retaining fixed-length SIDs as generation targets. DECOR [23] preserves token assignments, combines frozen codebook embeddings with learnable collaborative embeddings, and refines token representations through contextual composition. However, the semantic organization of SIDs does not by itself ensure that the generator learns the semantics of complete items and the relations among them.

2.2 Inter-item Relation Modeling

Discriminative recommenders exploit inter-item relations through transition structures, representation geometry, and ranking supervision [13, 18, 38]. In LLM-based recommendation, explicit relation modeling is introduced through attention structures and collaborative supervision. IAM [44] alternates between attention layers restricted to tokens within each item title and across items, separating title semantics from collaborative relations. TCA [20] normalizes collaborative scores over prefix-compatible items and sums the probabilities of items sharing the same next token to construct soft labels for LLM-based item-title generation. Recent work also introduces relational supervision into GR. APAO [42] optimizes prefix rankings with pointwise or pairwise objectives and adaptively emphasizes underperforming prefixes, while GFlowGR [36] incorporates collaborative signals into item-level terminal rewards and guides SID generation through flow balance objectives. However, GR uses discrete SID tokens shared across items as its basic modeling units, rather than continuous representations of entire items or text tokens processed by pretrained LLMs. Relations among complete items must therefore be expressed through token composition and generation, yet the connection between item-level relations and token-level dependencies remains largely implicit in GR models.

actual_output:
The theoretical models explaining item preference distributions and KL divergence in Semantic ID (SID) prefix trees are primarily detailed in the paper "REGER: Modeling inter-item Relations with Semantic IDs for Generative Recommendation" (arXiv:2610.37584v1). 

In this work, item SIDs are organized into a prefix tree structure, where each leaf node corresponds to a unique item, and the paths from the root to the leaves specify the complete SIDs. The authors introduce two key theorems related to item preferences and KL divergence:

1. **Exact Preference Factorization (Theorem 4.1)**: This theorem states that the preference probability of any item can be exactly factorized into conditional distributions over legal next tokens. This factorization allows for a structured understanding of how item preferences can be derived from the relationships between items represented in the SID prefix tree.

2. **Hierarchical KL Decomposition (Theorem 4.2)**: This theorem provides a method to decompose the KL divergence between two item preference distributions (denoted as P and Q) into a weighted sum of conditional KL divergences over all nonterminal prefixes in the prefix tree. The weights correspond to the prefix probability mass under distribution P. This decomposition connects item-level preferences to the conditional distributions of next tokens, thereby facilitating a deeper analysis of user preferences and item relationships.

These theoretical foundations motivate the design of the Hierarchical Collaborative Preference Distillation (HCPD) method, which leverages these decompositions to align teacher and generator distributions during training, enhancing the model's ability to capture collaborative preferences among items [1][2][3].

- ❷ We establish a theoretical framework that exactly factorizes item preference distributions over SID prefix trees and decomposes itemlevel KL into weighted prefix-conditional KL terms. Building on this, we develop the HCPD objective to guide SID generation.
- ❸ Experiments on six real-world benchmarks demonstrate REGER's consistent gains from explicit inter-item relation modeling and validate the effectiveness and efficiency of HCPD.

2 Related Work

2.1 Generative Recommendation

GR uses item tokenization to encode prior knowledge of inter-item relations into SIDs. TIGER [31] pioneered the use of residual quanti- zation in GR to learn semantic codes by reconstructing item content representations. Subsequent research has focused on incorporating collaborative signals into SID and aligning tokenization with recommendation objectives. LETTER [34] introduces collaborative alignment and code diversity regularization, while ETEGRec [22] alternates between tokenizer and recommender updates using alignment objectives. Other studies reconsider how item tokens are organized and represented. ActionPiece [11] learns merge rules over unordered feature sets using co-occurrences within items and across adjacent interactions. SST [26] compresses history-side item tokens into semantic subwords while retaining fixed-length SIDs as generation targets. DECOR [23] preserves token assignments, combines frozen codebook embeddings with learnable collaborative embeddings, and refines token representations through contextual composition. However, the semantic organization of SIDs does not by itself ensure that the generator learns the semantics of complete items and the relations among them.

2.2 Inter-item Relation Modeling

Discriminative recommenders exploit inter-item relations through transition structures, representation geometry, and ranking supervision [13, 18, 38]. In LLM-based recommendation, explicit relation modeling is introduced through attention structures and collaborative supervision. IAM [44] alternates between attention layers restricted to tokens within each item title and across items, separating title semantics from collaborative relations. TCA [20] normalizes collaborative scores over prefix-compatible items and sums the probabilities of items sharing the same next token to construct soft labels for LLM-based item-title generation. Recent work also introduces relational supervision into GR. APAO [42] optimizes prefix rankings with pointwise or pairwise objectives and adaptively emphasizes underperforming prefixes, while GFlowGR [36] incorporates collaborative signals into item-level terminal rewards and guides SID generation through flow balance objectives. However, GR uses discrete SID tokens shared across items as its basic modeling units, rather than continuous representations of entire items or text tokens processed by pretrained LLMs. Relations among complete items must therefore be expressed through token composition and generation, yet the connection between item-level relations and token-level dependencies remains largely implicit in GR models.

input: Identify the nuanced research inquiries driving the exploration of visual precision and semantic decomposition.
actual_output:
The exploration of visual precision and semantic decomposition in the context of multimodal models is driven by several nuanced research inquiries outlined in the paper "VAD: Attributing Visual Evidence for Target Reconstruction in Multimodal On-Policy Distillation" (arXiv:2607.28590v1). 

Firstly, the research questions focus on whether the proposed Visual Evidence Attribution Distillation (VAD) method enhances fine-grained visual accuracy compared to traditional post-training baselines (RQ1). This inquiry is crucial for understanding the effectiveness of VAD in improving visual perception capabilities.

Secondly, the study investigates how VAD influences the distribution of semantic content within the model's outputs. Specifically, it examines whether the decomposition process concentrates visual evidence in the attributed correction while shifting broader linguistic and teacher-specific semantics elsewhere (RQ2). This question is significant as it aims to determine if VAD effectively reallocates decision-relevant content rather than merely adjusting the original corrections.

Additionally, the research explores the impact of different supervision targets on the model's accuracy and its ability to support correct-token identification and wrong-token suppression (RQ3). This inquiry is essential for assessing how various training strategies can optimize model performance.

The generalization of checkpoints produced by different post-training algorithms to held-out tasks is another area of investigation (RQ4), which addresses the robustness and adaptability of the models.

Lastly, the study examines how factors such as supervision divergence, regularization weight, and positive-branch cap affect training outcomes (RQ5). This inquiry is vital for fine-tuning the training process and understanding the interplay of various hyperparameters in model performance.

Together, these inquiries form a comprehensive framework for evaluating and enhancing visual precision and semantic decomposition in multimodal learning systems.

Probing Spatial State Representations in Visual Foundation Models

Section: 5 Related Work Probing spatial and 3D structure in frozen representations. Frozen-feature probing asks what information is already accessible in a representation without updating the backbone. Self-supervised image encoders such as DINO and DINOv2 revealed that semantic organization, object boundaries, and strong local correspondences emerge without dense labels [6, 29]. More recent work extends this methodology to video foundation models: VidFM3D evaluates whether shallow readouts recover depth, camera pose, and 3D point structure from frozen video-model features, and analyzes how these signals vary with network depth and diffusion timestep [15]. Related probes of image foundation models test depth, surface normals, and multi-view correspondence [11], scene-level tasks such as 3D question answering, visual grounding, and registration [25], and novel-view synthesis from features read out as 3D Gaussians [9]. Feed-forward 3D reconstruction models, from DUSt3R to VGGT and Fast3R, provide a geometry-specialized reference point because their training directly targets multi-view reconstruction and camera estimation [35, 37, 38]; streaming variants such as Spann3R and CUT3R carry an explicit spatial memory or a persistent state that is updated with every new frame [34, 36]. Our streaming prefixes ask a related question of general-purpose representations without assuming such a state. Our work starts from the same evidence-first principle but changes the object of evaluation: metric geometry is one functional diagnostic rather than a definition of spatial state, and we also ask whether a representation supports view consistency, object persistence, predictive spatial update, and actionability. Two models with similar depth readout can therefore receive very different spatial-state profiles, and strong future-feature retrieval is not credited as predictive spatial update unless it passes matched motion controls. Internal representations of diffusion and video generation models. Large video generators such as Wan and CogVideoX are optimized for denoising and visual synthesis rather than for downstream readout [33, 41]. Nevertheless, work on image diffusion models has shown that semantic and geometric consistency can be extracted from internal activations, and that useful information is distributed across both network layers and diffusion timesteps [23, 31]. Recent probing of video diffusion transformers similarly reports that physical and 3D-related signals are most accessible at intermediate blocks and nontrivial noise levels [12, 15]. This motivates our layer × generation-coordinate × streaming-prefix analysis: we compare selected extraction settings rather than assuming that one hidden state characterizes an entire model. Such profiles describe accessibility during computation, not when a capability emerges during training. Spatial representations in foundation models. Spatial ability is often evaluated through language. SpatialVLM and SpatialRGPT improve quantitative and region-level spatial question answering by training vision-language models on large synthetic spatial data [7, 10], and VSI-Bench asks multimodal LLMs to remember and recall the layout of a space from video, finding that generating cognitive maps improves distance estimates [39]. Cambrian-S argues that such training alone does not yield robust implicit spatial representations and proposes predictive sensing, in which latent next-frame prediction decides what to remember [40]. A growing set of studies probes the representations themselves. SeeSE3 finds subspaces of self-supervised vision features that align with 3D Euclidean space, with camera motion linearly accessible from feature displacements [8]; SpaRRTa shows that visual foundation models differ markedly in how well they encode the relative positions of objects [19]; probes of V-JEPA 2 and VideoMAE-v2 decode camera motion best at 60-70% of network depth while intuitive physics stays near chance [28], and in video encoders, motion direction becomes decodable only within an intermediate-depth zone [16]. For multimodal LLMs, the spatial benefit of a visual representation tracks its 3D structure, measured by the cross-view consistency of latent features or the accuracy of explicit geometry [14]. This selective redistribution shows that the projection concentrates visually grounded, decision-relevant content rather than uniformly rescaling the teacher correction.
The token-level evidence confirms a semantic separation rather than a scalar rescaling. Figure 3(b) shows that every A-D answer symbol, together with representative attribute and object tokens such as vertical and metal , is more prominent in r vis t ; language scaffolding and artifact-related tokens such as to and inside are instead more prominent in r res t . The broader lexical profiles in Figure 3(c) exhibit the same organization: r vis t foregrounds colors, shapes, materials, spatial relations, objects, and answer choices, whereas r res t foregrounds linguistic realization and prompt- or degradation-related content. Taken together, the three views support the intended interpretation: r vis t carries the visually attributable evidence-to-decision signal, while r res t retains the portion of the teacher correction not explained by the visual intervention; the latter should therefore be interpreted as a mixed residual, not as purely linguistic noise.

Section: 2.2 Fine-Grained Visual Perception and Privileged Evidence

Instruction-tuned MLLMs support open-ended visual reasoning (Liu et al., 2023; Dai et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2023), while Qwen2-VL (Wang et al., 2024a), Qwen2.5-VL (Bai et al., 2025b), LLaVA-UHD (Xu et al., 2024), and Mini-Gemini (Li et al., 2024) improve native resolution or multi-scale detail. Nevertheless, diagnostic and high-resolution benchmarks continue to reveal failures on decisive local evidence (Tong et al., 2024b; Chen et al., 2024a; Wang et al., 2024b; Zhang et al., 2025b).
One strategy actively acquires better views: V* (Wu and Xie, 2023) and ZoomEye (Shen et al., 2025) search image regions, ReFocus (Fu et al., 2025) edits images as visual thoughts, and DeepEyes (Zheng et al., 2026), Thyme (Zhang et al., 2025a), DeepEyesV2 (Hong et al., 2026), and SenseNova-MARS (Chng et al., 2026) invoke image operations or multimodal tools. These methods expose fine detail at the cost of inference-time search or tool use.
Region-to-image training instead internalizes privileged local evidence. Zooming without Zooming (Wei et al., 2026) distills region-centric perception into a full-image pass; Vision-OPD (Yuan et al., 2026) uses a crop-conditioned selfteacher along student rollouts; and ViCuR (Tian et al., 2026) trains the student to recover privileged visual cues. Whereas these works improve evidence acquisition or representation, VAD addresses target construction by excluding teacher changes not explained by the revealed evidence.

Training setup. We train Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B on the same 6 , 241 synthetic visual question-answering examples released by Vision-OPD (Yuan et al., 2026); no training image or question overlaps the six primary benchmarks. Each example provides a full image x 0 with the relevant region marked, an evidence-present 2 × crop x + , and an evidence-degraded view x -obtained by 0 . 1 × bilinear downsampling and nearest-neighbor upsampling of that crop. The latter two views share region and size but differ in fine-grained evidence. A frozen copy of the initial student serves as teacher. VAD (Attributing Visual Evidence for Target Reconstruction in Multimodal On-Policy Distillation) demonstrates significant improvements in visual accuracy compared to other post-training methods. Specifically, VAD achieves higher average accuracies on fine-grained visual benchmarks, outperforming scale-matched alternatives by notable margins. For instance, at the 4B scale, VAD reaches an average accuracy of 78.32, which is 2.40 points higher than the best scale-matched alternative and 2.95 points higher than the closely related Decomposed OPD baseline. input: What training objectives do TCA and TCA-Aux optimize in recommendation systems?
actual_output:
TCA (Teacher-Student Collaborative Attention) and TCA-Aux (TCA with Auxiliary Loss) optimize different training objectives in recommendation systems. TCA-Aux enhances the cross-entropy (CE) loss with a Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence loss that utilizes full-vocabulary student probabilities. This approach aims to improve the model's performance by penalizing insufficient legal probability mass among the generated recommendations.

In contrast, TCA focuses on matching the teacher's conditional preferences without the auxiliary KL loss. Specifically, TCA renormalizes the student distribution over legal branches at each ground-truth prefix, directly aligning the student’s outputs with the teacher’s preferences. This method emphasizes capturing coarse-to-fine preference relations among catalog items, which is critical for effective collaborative preference supervision during training [1. arXiv:2610.37584v1].

The differences in their objectives are significant. While TCA-Aux imposes an additional penalty for the distribution of probabilities, TCA's approach is more straightforward, focusing on the direct matching of preferences without the added complexity of auxiliary losses. This distinction is crucial for understanding how these models leverage collaborative preferences to enhance recommendation performance [2. arXiv:2610.37584v1].
expected_output: TCA and TCA-Aux optimize weighted token likelihood and augment cross-entropy (CE) with a full-vocabulary auxiliary KL loss, respectively, using token-level soft labels derived from collaborative item scores.

A.2 Baselines

Main baselines. We organize the main baselines into three groups: (1) Discriminative recommendation: SASRec [14] uses unidirectional self-attention to model interaction sequences for next-item prediction. FDSA [43] separately models item-level and feature-level transitions through self-attention. BERT4Rec [32] employs bidirectional self-attention with a masked item prediction objective. S 3 -Rec [49] uses self-supervised pretraining to capture correlations among attributes, items, and sequences. DuoRec [29] combines dropout-based augmentation and supervised contrastive learning to alleviate representation degeneration. (2) Generative recommendation: TIGER [31] quantizes item content embeddings into SIDs using RQ-VAE and autoregressively generates the next item's SID. LETTER[34]combines semantic reconstruction, collaborative alignment, and diversity regularization to learn item codes. EAGER [35] uses separate behavioral and semantic generation streams with cross-stream information transfer. UNGER [40] integrates semantic and collaborative information into unified item codes through alignment and knowledge distillation. ReSID [19] constructs semantic IDs from structured item features through field-aware masked autoencoding and globally aligned orthogonal quantization. ETEGRec [22] alternately optimizes its tokenizer and recommender through sequence-item and preference-semantic alignment. DIGER [5] jointly learns semantic IDs and recommendation through differentiable quantization with decaying Gumbel noise. ActionPiece [11] constructs contextual tokens by merging frequently cooccurring features within items and across adjacent interactions. TIGER-SST [26] applies semantic subword tokenization to TIGER's history inputs while preserving fixed-length target SIDs. (3) Hybrid recommendation: LIGER [41] combines SID generation with dense retrieval to support candidate reranking and cold-start recommendation. MemGen-GR [2] adaptively combines generative and item-ID-based recommenders using a memorization-aware indicator to determine ensemble weights for each instance.

Each conditional KL compares the full distributions over all legal next tokens, including alternatives to the ground-truth token. Legal branches represent disjoint subsets of catalog items, so matching their probabilities provides explicit supervision on inter-item collaborative preferences. actual_output:
REGER demonstrates superior performance on both Recall@K (R@K) and NDCG@K (N@K) metrics compared to various generative and hybrid recommendation baselines. In the evaluations on the Amazon Reviews 2014 benchmarks, REGER outperforms all generative and hybrid baselines across three datasets and all metrics. Notably, it even surpasses DuoRec, a strong discriminative recommender, in most settings, although on the Toys dataset, REGER's Recall remains lower than DuoRec's, while it achieves comparable or slightly better NDCG [1. arXiv:2610.37584v1].

Specifically, REGER's ability to incorporate inter-item semantic and collaborative relations into its generative framework is highlighted as a key factor in its effectiveness. The results indicate that REGER consistently outperforms methods that attempt to integrate semantic and collaborative information, such as UNGER and ETEGRec, across all datasets [2. arXiv:2610.37584v1]. Furthermore, when compared to hybrid recommendation models like LIGER and MemGen-GR, REGER also shows superior performance, relying solely on its SID generation at inference [2. arXiv:2610.37584v1].

In the more recent Amazon Reviews 2023 benchmarks, REGER continues to achieve the best or second-best results across all metrics, reinforcing its capability in learning inter-item collaborative preferences within generative recommendation settings [3. arXiv:2610.37584v1]. Overall, these findings underscore REGER's strength in recommendation tasks, particularly through its innovative approach to modeling inter-item relations.

Section: B Results on Amazon Reviews 2023

REGER achieves the best or second-best results across all metrics on the larger 2023 benchmarks (Table 6), highlighting the value of learning inter-item collaborative preferences within GR. Although its teacher DuoRec trails recent generative baselines, HCPD consistently improves REGER. Interestingly, these gains persist on Scientific even though DuoRec underperforms REGER w/o HCPD on every metric. These results show that a teacher's top𝐾 recom- mendation performance does not fully reflect the supervisory value of its preference distribution. We attribute these gains to DuoRec's ability to capture each user's relative preferences among candidate items through discriminative item representations, providing supervision complementary to observed interactions. Furthermore, comparisons with TopoTok, DECOR, and Latte highlight the importance of translating inter-item relations into user-specific generation probabilities: semantically related items may differ in relevance to a user, and explicit preference supervision helps the generator distinguish among competing candidates.

input: Examine the synergistic elements of ExpertFlow that optimize Mixture-of-Experts inference performance.
actual_output:
ExpertFlow optimizes Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference performance through a synergistic integration of three key components: the Routing Path Predictor, the Token Scheduler, and the Predictive Expert Cache.

1. **Routing Path Predictor**: This transformer-based component estimates expert usage across all MoE layers in a single forward pass. By accurately predicting which experts will be needed for a given input, it enhances the efficiency of expert selection and utilization.

2. **Token Scheduler**: This element groups tokens with similar predicted routes, which improves expert utilization. By scheduling tokens in a way that aligns with predicted expert needs, the system minimizes unnecessary expert activations and maximizes throughput.

3. **Predictive Expert Cache**: This cache dynamically loads only the required experts based on the predictions from the Routing Path Predictor. It also corrects any mispredictions at runtime, ensuring that the system remains responsive and efficient even when initial predictions are not entirely accurate.

Together, these components enable ExpertFlow to achieve significant reductions in GPU memory usage—up to 93.72%—and improve inference throughput by up to 10 times compared to existing offloading methods. This efficiency is particularly valuable in memory-constrained environments, such as single-GPU setups, where traditional MoE models face challenges due to high parameter memory requirements [1][4][5].

In summary, the coordinated operation of these three components not only enhances expert utilization but also facilitates early expert planning and reduces CPU-GPU transfer overhead, positioning ExpertFlow as a robust solution for scalable and efficient MoE deployment [1][5].

We introduced ExpertFlow , a unified system for memory-efficient MoE inference under tight GPU constraints. By integrating a Routing Path Predictor , a routing-aware Token Scheduler , and a predictive Expert Cache Engine , ExpertFlow enables early expert planning, higher expert utilization, and reduced CPU-GPU transfers, yielding up to 93.72% peak memory reduction and up to 10 × throughput improvement across diverse MoE architectures when compared with strong offloading baselines. Accurate routing prediction also shows broader value for distributed expert placement, routing-guided pruning, and hierarchical caching, positioning ExpertFlow as a foundation for future system-level co-design that incorporates predictive routing into scalable sparse model deployment and training.

1 Introduction

Sparse MoE models [5, 8, 14, 25] scale parameter size efficiently by activating only a small subset of experts per input, reducing pertoken computation while keeping accuracy comparable to dense LLMs [10, 21, 22]. This efficiency, however, increases memory usage. For instance, Mixtral-8 × 7B [14] requires more than 96 GB of GPU memory, exceeding the 80 GB capacity of an NVIDIA A100 GPU. Although 45.1B of its 46.7B parameters belong to expert modules, only a small fraction is used per input, leading to substantial memory redundancy. This sparsity suggests that offloading inactive experts to CPU and loading only the needed ones can reduce GPU memory demand. Existing studies have investigated such offloading methods [6, 7, 12, 15, 27, 35], but remain limited by three challenges.

Low expert utilization. In the decoding phase, the token distribution across experts can be highly imbalanced, and some experts may receive only a single token. Since expert kernels have nearconstant cost when handling a small number of tokens [32], such sparse assignments lead to low compute efficiency.

Inefficient expert prediction. Early and accurate expert activation prediction underpins effective offloading, as it enables scheduling and prefetching before experts are required. Prior work takes two routes. Regression-based methods [6, 12] approximate router scores, but even small score errors can affect output quality, necessitating extensive fine-tuning to recover the original routing. Classification-based methods predict selected experts directly. Heuristic variants based on token-expert statistics [14, 17, 34] are lightweight but fail to capture input-dependent routing behavior. Learning-based predictors (e.g., ProMoE [27]) improve accuracy, yet their layer-by-layer sequential design reveals expert usage only after the previous layer executes, restricting scheduling flexibility.

Ineffective expert caching. Expert caching is central to controlling GPU memory usage. The commonly used LRU policy [7] evicts experts purely by recency and overlooks routing patterns, leading to unstable cache hit rates under MoE's dynamic activations. SE-MoE [35] improves locality by caching all experts from two consecutive layers through a ring-buffer design, but this creates large memory overhead for models with many experts (e.g., Switch128) and repeatedly loads inactive experts, resulting in unnecessary CPU-GPU transfers.

3.1 System Design Overview

Deploying MoE models under tight memory budgets, such as singleGPU settings, is challenging due to dynamic expert routing, low expert utilization, and heavy parameter movement. These issues are interdependent: inaccurate routing prediction limits scheduling, fragmented token batches activate unnecessary experts, and poor memory planning amplifies transfer overhead. ExpertFlow addresses these challenges through a unified design that integrates a routing path predictor ( RPP ), a token scheduler ( TS ), and an expert cache engine ( ECE ). The RPP provides early global routing signals, enabling the TS to reorganize tokens by predicted paths and the ECE to prefetch only the required experts. 3.2 Routing Path Predictor (RPP)

3.2.1 Predictor Architecture. Existing predictors [12, 27] use MLPs to infer expert choices layer by layer, creating a sequential dependency that prevents early scheduling and prefetching. ExpertFlow replaces this design with a T5-style encoder-decoder architecture [22] (Fig. 2). The encoder embeds the full input sequence, and the decoder generates routing predictions in one pass. We attach 𝐿 lightweight heads to the decoder, each producing logits over 𝐸 experts for a specific MoE layer. Sparse MoE models [5, 8, 14, 25] scale parameter size efficiently by activating only a small subset of experts per input, reducing pertoken computation while keeping accuracy comparable to dense LLMs [10, 21, 22]. Although 45.1B of its 46.7B parameters belong to expert modules, only a small fraction is used per input, leading to substantial memory redundancy. This sparsity suggests that offloading inactive experts to CPU and loading only the needed ones can reduce GPU memory demand. Existing studies have investigated such offloading methods [6, 7, 12, 15, 27, 35], but remain limited by three challenges.

Low expert utilization. In the decoding phase, the token distribution across experts can be highly imbalanced, and some experts may receive only a single token. Since expert kernels have nearconstant cost when handling a small number of tokens [32], such sparse assignments lead to low compute efficiency.

Inefficient expert prediction. Early and accurate expert activation prediction underpins effective offloading, as it enables scheduling and prefetching before experts are required. Prior work takes two routes. Learning-based predictors (e.g., ProMoE [27]) improve accuracy, yet their layer-by-layer sequential design reveals expert usage only after the previous layer executes, restricting scheduling flexibility.

Abstract

Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models can outperform dense large language models at similar computation by activating only a small set of experts per token. However, stacking many expert modules introduces substantial parameter memory, which makes MoE models difficult to deploy in memory-constrained environments such as single-GPU devices. Offloading alleviates this issue by storing inactive experts in CPU memory and loading them on demand, but existing methods remain limited: static caches disregard input-dependent routing, and methods that train separate models to predict expert usage ahead of time are often inaccurate or require significant training cost. We propose ExpertFlow , a lightweight MoE inference system that addresses this routing dependency through three coordinated components: 1) a transformerbased routing path predictor that estimates expert usage across all MoElayers in a single forward pass, 2) a token scheduler that groups tokens with similar predicted routes to improve expert utilization, and 3) a predictive expert cache that loads only the required experts while correcting mispredictions at runtime. Together, these components enable efficient expert loading and execution, reducing GPU memory usage by up to 93.72% and improving inference throughput

by up to 10 × over strong offloading baselines on a single GPU.

Model offloading reduces GPU memory usage by moving model states or computations to cheaper storage or processing units. Early work such as ZeRO [23, 24] offloaded optimizer states, gradients, and weights to CPUs or SSDs during training, and later extensions applied similar ideas to inference [3, 26, 28]. However, these methods are designed for dense LLMs and do not handle the dynamic, input-dependent routing of MoE models. Existing MoE offloading approaches either rely on low-accuracy heuristics [7, 17] or require costly predictor training [6, 12], limiting practical adoption. In contrast, we develop a unified system that provides accurate and low-cost expert routing prediction, enabling more efficient and flexible MoE inference.

actual_output:
PAC-MAN integrates safety and perception constraints through a framework that combines control barrier functions (CBFs) with perception-aware reinforcement learning (RL) to enable effective humanoid dodgeball evasion. The central challenge addressed by PAC-MAN is the need for the humanoid robot to avoid contact with an incoming ball while maintaining balance, using only limited onboard sensing capabilities.

The framework employs CBFs to encode safety constraints, allowing the robot to determine collision-free movements. However, these functions rely on the availability of relevant state information, which is often limited in real-world scenarios where the robot perceives the ball only through a depth camera. To mitigate this, PAC-MAN incorporates two levels of barrier guidance: Link-CBF, which provides lightweight per-link rewards during training, and Joint-CBF, a more comprehensive whole-body projection that can guide training or serve as a runtime filter during deployment. This dual approach allows the robot to internalize safety structures based on the perceptual information it receives, which is crucial given the transient nature of the dodgeball threat [1][5].

Additionally, PAC-MAN utilizes an adversarial motion prior (AMP) to regularize the robot's evasive movements, encouraging reflex-like actions such as crouching, leaning, and sidestepping, rather than arbitrary joint movements. This regularization helps ensure that the evasive maneuvers are both effective and natural [1][2].

The evaluation of PAC-MAN shows that the performance of the robot in evading balls improves significantly with better perceptual observability. For instance, the Joint-CBF performs best when accurate ball states are available, while the Link-CBF is more suitable for deployment under limited perception conditions, demonstrating the importance of integrating safety and perception in real-time applications [2][3].

The closest conceptual neighbor to perception-aware dodgeball is safe agility under partial exteroception. Quadruped parkour [23], [24] and agile-but-safe locomotion [8] show how perception, skill selection, recovery, and safety layers can support fast motion around obstacles, while humanoid parkour and perception-aware locomotion systems [2], [25][27] extend this to higher-dimensional bodies with depthor elevation-conditioned policies for jumping, leaping, and terrain traversal. Related work studies the same perception-speed-stability tradeoff through depth conditioning [7], online policy switching [28], and active gaze [29]. Dodgeball differs from these terrain-centered settings because the hazard is a fast-moving object rather than traversable terrain. The ball may be visible only briefly, so the policy must forecast imminent body contact and produce an evasive whole-body response instead of merely choosing footholds. Task-centered fast-object work makes this timing pressure explicit: [30] uses humanoid table tennis to study sub-second ball prediction, task planning, and whole-body RL control. Dodgeball shares the timing but changes the objective from striking to avoiding contact. This shift stresses egocentric observability: an onboard depth camera must provide enough information for the body to leave the ball's path before impact.
Whole-body avoidance and safety. Reactive safety spans both recovering balance after a disturbance via capture-point and push-recovery control [31], [32], and avoiding contact in the first place via control barrier functions [10], collisionfree MPC [33], and fast collision-free motion generation [34]. The Link-CBF policy demonstrates significant efficacy in evading projectiles while maintaining balance during humanoid dodgeball trials. In simulations, the policy was evaluated under various conditions, including a fixed-camera setup and a gimbal-mounted camera, with results indicating that the Link-CBF policy outperformed the no-barrier baseline. Specifically, it achieved a success rate of 90% in the reset regime and 89% in the deployment regime, which involves the robot returning to its original position between throws. This performance is notably higher than the bare Joint-CBF, which dropped to 76% in the deployment regime, suggesting that the Link-CBF effectively extends safety guidance from just pelvis clearance to every body link, enhancing overall evasion capabilities [1][2].

The policy relied solely on onboard depth perception and semantic segmentation to identify and evade different projectiles, demonstrating its robustness in real-world conditions despite the absence of ground-truth ball states or velocity estimates [4][5]. 

The design of the Link-CBF policy allows it to coordinate evasive maneuvers involving the legs, torso, and arms, rather than merely translating the base, which is crucial for maintaining balance while dodging [2]. The combination of effective perception and a well-structured safety mechanism enables the robot to respond appropriately to various projectile threats, thereby ensuring both evasion and stability during the trials [3]. 

Overall, the Link-CBF policy proves to be a reliable approach for humanoid robots in dodgeball scenarios, balancing the need for agility in evasion with the requirement to maintain an upright posture.

PAC-MAN: Perception-Aware CBF-RL for Whole-Body Safety in Humanoid Dodgeball

Lizhi Yang, Junheng Li and Aaron D. Ames

Abstract -We present PAC-MAN, a perception-aware CBFRL framework that couples control-barrier safety with deployment-realistic onboard sensing for whole-body humanoid dodgeball. The deployed policy sees the ball only as segmentation-masked depth from a head-mounted camera, while training-time CBF guidance represents clearance to every body link, and an adversarial motion prior regularizes the resulting evasive reflexes. We evaluate on a controlled anylink contact benchmark with seeded throws in two regimes: single throws and a deployment loop in which the robot walks back to its station and recovers between throws. On this benchmark, the policy comes within a few points of a privileged state oracle: a fixed onboard camera alone is adequate for evasion. We find that usable barrier structure depends on perceptual observability: Joint-CBF gives the best performance with accurate ball states, degrades under fixedcamera observations when used only as training guidance, and recovers with a ball-tracking gimbal or privileged runtime filter. We therefore deploy a lightweight Link-CBF policy zero-shot on the Unitree G1 in the real world, where it tolerates imperfect perception, succeeds on 95 % of throws, and uses semantic segmentation to dodge different balls.

I. INTRODUCTION

Humanoid robots operating around moving objects must react within a fraction of a second, and the evasion itself must not cost them their balance. Dodgeball isolates this safety problem in a short-horizon, whole-body setting: the robot must perceive an incoming ball, determine which links are threatened, and coordinate the torso, arms, and legs quickly enough to avoid contact while remaining upright. Humans solve the same problem by keeping their eyes on the ball and moving their whole body out of its path. Recent learning-based controllers can produce dynamic humanoid locomotion [1], [2], whole-body imitation [3]-[5], and visually conditioned skills [6], [7], but reactive whole-body safety from onboard vision remains difficult [8], [9], especially for a humanoid.

Control barrier functions (CBFs) encode collision-free sets and correct unsafe commands, provided the relevant state is available [10]. Onboard perception breaks this convenient assumption: the incoming object may be visible only briefly, may leave the camera field of view, or may appear as a few noisy depth pixels. CBF-RL can move barrier information into policy training [11], but a deployed policy can internalize only as much safety structure as its observations support. The threat representation and the barrier design therefore

Unlike navigation around a mapped obstacle, the hazard is transient, and the robot has no nominal velocity command or reference motion that specifies when and how to evade. The short observation window and whole-body collision geometry make dodgeball a direct test of safety under partial observation.

We present PAC-MAN, a perception-aware CBF-RL framework for humanoid dodgeball. The central question is how much barrier structure a policy can internalize when it receives only deployment-realistic observations. PAC-MAN studies two levels: Link-CBF, a lightweight per-link reward used during training, and Joint-CBF, a stronger whole-body joint-space projection that can either guide training or stay active at test time as a privileged runtime filter. The two levels separate learned barrier-guided behavior from online barrier enforcement.

How well the learned reflex works depends on what perception tells the policy about the threat. The deployed system segments the ball in RGB and masks the depth image down to a compact ball-only observation. An adversarial motion prior (AMP) regularizes how the humanoid moves, so the evasions come out as crouches, leans, sidesteps, and leaps; the safety structure itself comes from the CBF terms.

input: Compare the construction methods of uniform, normal-quantile, and Lloyd-Max codebook families, highlighting their unique approaches.
actual_output:
The construction methods for the three codebook families—uniform, normal-quantile, and Lloyd-Max—each employ distinct approaches to generate representative values for embeddings.

1. **Uniform Codebooks**: This method places values at equal intervals between -1 and 1. For example, with two bits, the values are {-1, -1/3, 1/3, 1}. An alternative variant, termed Uniform*, includes zero and uses K-1 equally spaced values, resulting in {-1, 0, 1} for two bits. This straightforward approach ensures a uniform distribution of values across the specified range, which can be beneficial for certain applications [1].

2. **Normal-Quantile Codebooks**: In contrast, normal-quantile codebooks focus on the quantiles of a standard normal distribution, which allows for a concentration of values near zero. For more than two bits, the values are derived from quantiles at specific probabilities, but for two bits, a fixed codebook of {-1, -0.3186, 0.3186, 1} is used. This method is particularly advantageous for embeddings that exhibit a distribution skewed towards zero, as it captures more detail in that region [1].

3. **Lloyd-Max Codebooks**: This approach is adaptive, as it learns the codebook values directly from the distribution of the trained embeddings. Initially, embeddings are normalized to prevent magnitude differences from skewing the codebook. The Lloyd-Max algorithm involves two iterative steps: assigning sampled components to the nearest codebook value and updating the codebook values based on the mean of the assigned components. This method is particularly effective because it tailors the codebook to the specific characteristics of the embeddings, resulting in improved performance [1].

In summary, while uniform codebooks provide a simple and evenly distributed set of values, normal-quantile codebooks focus on capturing the central tendency of the data, and Lloyd-Max codebooks adaptively learn from the data distribution, making them potentially more effective for complex embeddings.

input: How are normalized embeddings applied to iteratively adjust Lloyd-Max codebook values during fitting?
actual_output:
In the process of fitting the Lloyd-Max codebook values, normalized embeddings play a crucial role. Initially, each embedding is normalized to ensure that differences in magnitude do not dominate the shared codebook. This normalization is achieved by calculating a scale based on the embedding's root mean square (RMS), which is clamped to avoid division by zero.

Once the embeddings are normalized, the fitting process involves two iterative steps. First, each sampled component from the normalized embeddings is assigned to its nearest codebook value. This assignment is denoted as \( a_j \), where \( j \) indexes the sampled components. The second step involves updating each codebook value by replacing it with the mean of the components assigned to it, represented as \( c_{\text{new}, k} \) for each codebook value \( k \). This update is contingent on the set of indices \( S_k \) that contains the sampled components assigned to that codebook value. If no components are assigned to a particular codebook value, it remains unchanged.

This iterative process is repeated for a total of 60 iterations, allowing the codebook values to converge towards a representation that better fits the distribution of the normalized components from the embeddings. The final fitted values are then stored in bfloat16 (BF16) format for further use in the model [1. arXiv:2610.31646v1].

input: How does VAD's functionality contribute to its superior performance compared to other models across multiple benchmarks?
actual_output:
VAD (Attributing Visual Evidence for Target Reconstruction in Multimodal On-Policy Distillation) demonstrates superior performance compared to other models due to its unique approach to visual evidence attribution and reconstruction. This method allows VAD to achieve higher fine-grained visual accuracy across various benchmarks. Specifically, VAD outperforms the best scale-matched alternatives by 2.40 points at the 4B scale and 2.80 points at the 9B scale, as well as exceeding the closely related Decomposed OPD baseline by 2.95 and 2.88 points, respectively [1. arXiv:2607.28590v1].

The effectiveness of VAD is attributed to its ability to isolate the benefits of attributing and reconstructing privileged corrections rather than relying solely on additional examples or updates. This results in consistent improvements in fine-detail localization, high-resolution perception, and real-world recognition across all evaluated benchmarks, rather than focusing on a single dataset [1. arXiv:2607.28590v1].
